question: A patient with a tibial plateau fracture develops increasing leg pain unresponsive to analgesia. Measured compartment pressure is 42 mmHg; diastolic BP is 68 mmHg. What is the correct action?

answers.text: Observe for 6 hours and remeasure compartment pressure

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Observation is dangerous when compartment pressure already exceeds the critical threshold — delay risks irreversible muscle necrosis.

Correct. ΔP = diastolic BP − compartment pressure = 68 − 42 = 26 mmHg, which is below the critical threshold of 30 mmHg. Emergency fasciotomy is indicated regardless of whether the distal pulse is present.

answers.text: Elevate the limb and apply ice packs

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Elevation reduces arterial perfusion pressure and can worsen compartment syndrome — it is contraindicated once the syndrome is established.

answers.text: Administer IV mannitol and monitor urine output

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Mannitol has no proven role in established compartment syndrome; the definitive treatment is surgical fasciotomy.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember: compartment syndrome is a clinical-pressure emergency. ΔP = diastolic BP − compartment pressure; if < 30 mmHg, fasciotomy is mandatory regardless of pulse status.
Well done. The ΔP (delta-P) criterion — diastolic BP minus compartment pressure < 30 mmHg — is the operative threshold. A palpable pulse does NOT exclude compartment syndrome.
